Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
The world is a dangerous place
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

vignette: Juan had always taken pride in his work as a prosecutor, known for his sharp mind and unwavering commitment to justice. But on one fateful evening, after a long day in court, his life took a devastating turn. He had stopped at a local bar to unwind with colleagues, but as the night wore on, he found himself alone, disoriented, and vulnerable. It was then that a stranger, someone he thought he could trust, took advantage of him, subjecting Juan to a brutal sexual assault. The details of that night are forever seared in Juan's memory - the sound of shattering glass, the feel of cold sweat on his skin, the stench of stale beer and desperation. Even now, years later, the recollection feels like it's happening all over again, transporting him back to a state of raw terror. He can't shake the feeling that he's reliving the assault every time the memory forces its way into his mind unbidden. As Juan navigates his daily life, certain triggers serve as painful reminders of that night. Being around children is especially difficult - their laughter and playful energy now evoke a sense of unease, making him feel like he's constantly on edge. He avoids taking his grandchildren to the park or attending school events, fearing that someone might notice his agitation and wonder what's wrong. Even being in close proximity to related people can be overwhelming; Juan feels like he's under scrutiny, as if they can see right through him. Simple sensory experiences have also become fraught with anxiety for Juan. A specific temperature on his skin - the kind of cool breeze that whispers across his neck - instantly transports him back to the moment of the assault. He finds himself flinching at the slightest touch or brush against his arm, as if his body is perpetually braced for impact. In an effort to cope with these triggers and regain a sense of control, Juan has developed several strategies. Whenever he enters a new room or building, he instinctively scans for exits, mentally mapping out potential escape routes. He notices objects that could be used as weapons - the heavy bookend on a shelf, the letter opener on his desk - and feels an involuntary jolt of fear. Avoiding unfamiliar places has become second nature; Juan is convinced that he can only truly assess danger if he knows the terrain. But these coping mechanisms come at a cost. Juan's world has shrunk dramatically since the assault. He no longer takes his morning walks through the neighborhood or meets friends for coffee. His work as a prosecutor, once so fulfilling, now feels isolating and overwhelming. The constant threat assessment is exhausting; Juan often finds himself wondering if he'll ever be able to let his guard down again. Despite his best efforts, Juan can't shake the feeling of being permanently damaged - that his body has been forever altered by what happened. He's consumed by a deep-seated sense of contamination, as if the very essence of who he is has been tainted. This self-perception seeps into every aspect of his life; even small gestures like shaking hands or sharing meals with loved ones feel tainted by an unspoken vulnerability. It was only when Juan's grandchildren began to notice his withdrawal that he realized something had to change. Their innocent questions - "Abuelo, why are you always so sad?" - pierced the armor he'd built around himself. Fearing that he'll lose them if he can't confront his demons, Juan has finally sought help. He's terrified of reliving the assault in therapy, but more afraid still of losing himself to its aftermath.
